notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 5
notes.body: ★ MORPHEME = smallest form + meaning/function pairing. WORD = smallest SEPARABLE unit (not the spelling definition). Complex = >1 morpheme. ★ ROOT (indivisible core) vs. BASE (what an affix attaches to) vs. AFFIX (bound). Affix types: PREFIX, SUFFIX, CIRCUMFIX, INFIX, SIMULTANEOUS. FREE (stands alone) vs. BOUND (must attach; only roots can be free). ★ BEYOND AFFIXES: internal change (mouse→mice), suppletion (go→went, memorized), reduplication (salad-salad). ★ TYPOLOGY: isolating/analytic vs. synthetic → agglutinative (separable, one-meaning) vs. fusional (one affix = many meanings). ★ ALLOMORPHY: allomorphs = variant forms; PHONOLOGICALLY conditioned (a/an; plural [s]/[z]/[ɪz]) vs. LEXICALLY conditioned (ox→oxen). ZERO affix = ∅. ★ LEXICAL CATEGORY defined by DISTRIBUTION, not meaning. ★ DERIVATION changes meaning/CATEGORY (new word); INFLECTION expresses grammatical info and NEVER changes category. ★ COMPOUND = 2+ ROOTS; English stress on FIRST member. ★ STRUCTURAL AMBIGUITY = one string, two structures/meanings (unlockable); shown with morphological TREES.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.9-5.11 Structure, trees & solving problems
notes.body: Words have internal structure, which can create structural ambiguity: one string with two possible structures and meanings (e.g., unlockable = 'able to be unlocked' [[un-lock]-able] vs. 'unable to be locked' [un-[lock-able]]). We show structure with morphological tree diagrams built by successive affixation. To solve an unfamiliar-language morphology problem, compare glossed forms, line up recurring form-meaning pairings, and isolate each morpheme's form, meaning, and position.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.8 Compounding
notes.body: Compounding builds a word from two or more roots (blackboard, dog-tired, dishwasher). English compounds freely across categories (N-N, Adj-N, V-N, etc.). Spelling is inconsistent (solid, hyphenated, or spaced), so it's an unreliable test; a better cue is stress — English compounds are stressed on the FIRST member (gréenhouse vs. green hóuse). Compounding differs from derivation and inflection because it combines roots rather than adding affixes.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.7 Inflectional morphology
notes.body: Inflectional morphology expresses grammatical information appropriate to a word's category and NEVER changes the category. English has a small inflectional system: noun plural -s and possessive -'s; verb 3rd-person-singular present -s, past -ed, and participles; adjective comparative -er / superlative -est. Other languages inflect far more (case, gender, agreement, tense/aspect/mood). Some 'inflectional' meanings can instead be shown syntactically (e.g., 'will' for future) — that's not inflectional morphology.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.6 Derivational morphology
notes.body: Derivational morphology changes the meaning and/or the lexical category of its base, building a new word: teach (V) + -er → teacher (N); happy (Adj) + -ness → happiness (N); un- + kind → unkind (meaning change, same category). Derivation is often not fully productive (idiosyncratic, with gaps) and typically sits closer to the root than inflection. It's how languages expand the lexicon.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.5 Lexical categories
notes.body: A lexical category (part of speech) is a group of words that behave the same for grammatical purposes. Crucially, linguists define categories by DISTRIBUTION (the grammatical contexts a word appears in), not by meaning — semantic tests ('a noun is a person/place/thing') fail on cases like action and event (both nouns). Tests for the four lexical categories (noun, verb, adjective, adverb) mix syntactic distribution (e.g., nouns follow determiners, can be subjects/objects, take plurals) and morphological behaviour. Morphology divides into derivational and inflectional, plus compounding.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.4 Allomorphy
notes.body: Allomorphy is when one morpheme (consistent meaning) has different forms (allomorphs) by environment. Phonologically conditioned allomorphy is chosen by nearby sounds: a/an, and the English plural surfacing as [s] (books), [z] (dogs), or [ɪz]/[əz] (nieces) based on the noun's final sound. Lexically conditioned allomorphy is tied to the specific root and must be memorized: child→children, ox→oxen, mouse→mice, sheep→sheep. A form with no overt marking is a zero affix, written ∅ (plural of sheep/deer). English plural allomorphs: -s, -z, -ɪz, -(r)en, internal change, -∅.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.3 Morphology beyond affixes
notes.body: Some processes don't add an affix: internal change (sounds inside the root change — mouse→mice, sit→sat; irregular relics of old regular patterns), suppletion (the form is wholly replaced — go→went, good→better→best; always memorized, often on frequent words), and reduplication (repeating part/all of a word — Halq'eméylem qwélqwel 'talkative'; English 'salad-salad' = prototypical example). Morphological typology: isolating/analytic (few morphemes per word — Mandarin) vs. synthetic (much word-internal morphology), which splits into agglutinative (many separable one-meaning affixes — Japanese) vs. fusional (one affix fuses many meanings — Spanish -áramos).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.2 Roots, bases, and affixes
notes.body: An affix is a bound morpheme that must attach to a base; the base can be simple or complex (library → librarian → librarianship). A root is the smallest, indivisible base. Affix types: prefix (before, inter-), suffix (after, -s), circumfix (around, Meskwaki ne-…-ena·n), infix (inside another morpheme, Tagalog -um-), and simultaneous affix (at the same time — signed motion, or a tonal/stress morpheme like récord/recórd). Cross-cutting distinction: free morphemes stand alone (cat); bound morphemes cannot (all affixes + bound roots like -whelmed). Only roots can be free; bound morphemes are written with a hyphen on the attaching side.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: 5.1 What is morphology?
notes.body: Morphology is the study of how words are built from smaller pieces. A word is the smallest separable unit — it can stand alone and reorder in a sentence (a linguistic definition, not the orthographic 'spaces' one, since not all languages are written or spaced). Linguists distinguish phonological, morphological, and syntactic words. A morpheme is the smallest systematic pairing of form and meaning-or-grammatical-function (cat, -s). Words with more than one morpheme are morphologically complex (cats, non-renew-abil-ity); one-morpheme words are simple. Whether a word is complex depends on how today's speakers analyze it, not its etymology.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: Chapter 5 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 5 you should be able to: define morphemes and identify them in words; distinguish roots, bases, and affixes (and affix types); recognize non-affixal morphology (internal change, suppletion, reduplication) and morphological typology; analyze allomorphy; identify lexical categories by distribution; distinguish derivational from inflectional morphology; and analyze compounds and structural ambiguity, including drawing morphological trees.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 4
notes.body: ★ PHONEME /x/ (abstract) = a set of ALLOPHONES [x] (physical), each in its ENVIRONMENT. Notation: / / phonemic, [ ] phonetic, < > spelling. ★ English /t/: [ɾ] before UNstressed vowel (atom), [tʰ] before STRESSED vowel (atomic). ★ CONTRASTIVE distribution (overlap) ⇒ DIFFERENT phonemes; one MINIMAL PAIR proves it. COMPLEMENTARY distribution (no overlap) ⇒ same OR different phonemes — decide by PHONETIC SIMILARITY ([iː]/[i] same phoneme; [h]/[ŋ] different). ★ No minimal pair? Use NEAR-minimal pairs (need several) or NONCE words. ★ NATURAL CLASS = shared properties + shared behaviour, must be EXHAUSTIVE + language-specific. PHONOTACTICS = allowable combinations. ★ RULE template A → B / C _ D (target → change / environment); _ = position, # = word edge. FAITHFULNESS = default allophone elsewhere; SIMPLICITY = fewest rules. ★ UR /phonemes/ → (rules) → SR [phones] = DERIVATION (table: UR top, rules side, SR bottom, — = no apply). ★ ASSIMILATION = change matches environment (phonation/place/nasality). ★ Signed languages lack fully PRODUCTIVE rules; have sign processes: weak hand FREEZE, weak hand DROP, LOWERING. Symmetry Condition = two-handed moving signs share handshape + movement.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.10 Signed language phonology
notes.body: Spoken-language phonological rules are typically fully productive (no exceptions). Signed languages don't seem to have such productive rules — perhaps because there's no phone-like unit between parameters and syllable/sign to target. They do have rule-like processes affecting individual signs, especially effort-reducing ones on two-handed signs: weak hand freeze (nondominant hand stops moving), weak hand drop (nondominant hand deleted), and lowering (sign made at a lower, easier location). Reminder: analyze signed languages in their own right, not by importing spoken-language analysis.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.9 Types of phonological rules
notes.body: The most common type is assimilation — a phoneme changes to match a property of its environment: phonation assimilation (French sonorant devoicing; Wemba Wemba post-nasal voicing; Polish regressive devoicing), place assimilation (Persian alveolar→postalveolar before postalveolar), and nasality assimilation (Ka'apor vowels nasalized after a nasal stop). Other rule types include dissimilation, deletion, epenthesis (insertion), and metathesis (reordering).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.8 Phonological derivations
notes.body: A derivation demonstrates the analysis: build each word's UR (identical to SR except where a rule applies, per faithfulness), then run a derivation table — URs across the top, named rules down the side, SRs across the bottom, with — where a rule doesn't apply. Good demonstrations include words where the rule applies (a representative spread of the target class), words where it doesn't (wrong environment), and similar phonemes in the right environment that are unaffected.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.7 Phonological rules
notes.body: Rather than list a default statement for every phoneme, we rely on faithfulness: a phoneme surfaces as its default allophone anywhere no rule applies. Remaining patterns are captured as phonological rules using natural classes. A rule has the template A → B / C _ D: target (natural class A) → change (properties B) / environment (C _ D), with _ = the target's position and # = a word boundary (e.g., 'sonorant → voiceless / voiceless-obstruent _ #'). In generative phonology, words have an underlying representation (UR, /phonemes/) and a surface representation (SR, [phones]); rules 'generate' the SR from the UR.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.5-4.6 Phonemic analysis
notes.body: Phonemic analysis = working out a language's phonemes, allophones, and distributions; the result is a phonemicization (not unique — multiple analyses can fit). Procedure: list the phones of interest, find their environments, decide contrastive vs. complementary, and group them. When analyses tie on the data, apply the principle of simplicity (fewest statements). Worked examples in the text include Georgian laterals ([l] vs. [ɫ]) and Canadian French sonorant devoicing.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.4 Complementary distribution
notes.body: Two phones with non-overlapping environments are in complementary distribution — but that alone doesn't tell you the phoneme count. [h] and [ŋ] are complementary yet feel like different consonants (little phonetic similarity → different phonemes). Long [iː] and short [i] are complementary AND phonetically similar (same quality, differ only in length) → allophones of one phoneme /i/. Decision tool: phonetic similarity. Key result: contrastive distribution ⇒ different phonemes; complementary distribution ⇒ could be same or different phonemes.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.3 Contrastive distribution & minimal pairs
notes.body: Two phones with overlapping distributions contrast → contrastive distribution → different phonemes. A single minimal pair (identical except one position, different meaning: pill/kill) proves contrast. When true minimal pairs are scarce (e.g., rare [ʒ]), use near-minimal pairs (need several, since one could be misleading) or nonce words (invented words speakers judge). Larger sets are possible — English beet/bit/bait/bet/bat/but/bot/bought/boat/boot is a minimal 10-tuplet showing ten contrasting vowels at once.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.2 Phonotactics and natural classes
notes.body: Phonotactics = language-specific restrictions on allowable combinations (English bans [tl]/[dl] onsets; three-consonant onsets must be [s] + voiceless plosive + approximant). Restrictions aren't random — they target natural classes: sets of phones sharing phonetic properties and phonological behaviour. Natural classes must be exhaustive (include every qualifying phone in that language), so membership is language-specific ([p t k] are a natural class in English, but Kalaallisut's voiceless plosives also include [q]). In ASL, the Symmetry Condition is a phonotactic constraint on two-handed moving signs (same handshape + movement).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: 4.1 Phonemes and allophones
notes.body: Phonology studies the patterns governing which unit combinations are valid and what changes occur when units combine (spoken and signed). A phoneme is an abstract category (in / /) that speakers treat as one sound; its physical realizations are allophones (in [ ]), each used in a particular environment. English /t/ surfaces as flap [ɾ] before an unstressed vowel (atom, data, writer) but aspirated [tʰ] before a stressed vowel (atomic, attack, return). Phonemes are abstractions we infer from distributional patterns — the core work of phonology is figuring out a language's phonemes, their allophones, and each allophone's environment. Modality matters, so spoken and signed phonology are treated separately.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: Chapter 4 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 4 you should be able to: identify phonemes and their allophones; determine the distribution of phones (contrastive vs. complementary) using minimal pairs, near-minimal pairs, and nonce words; carry out a basic phonemic analysis; write phonological rules and derivations; and describe how signed-language phonology differs from spoken.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 3
notes.body: ★ MODALITY: spoken = vocal-auditory; signed = manual-visual. Phonetics studies ALL modalities. Subfields: articulatory (production), perceptual, acoustic. ★ CONSONANT = full description in order PHONATION–PLACE–MANNER. ★ ACTIVE (lower, moving) vs. PASSIVE (upper, target) articulator; PLACE = their combo (named active-first). ★ PHONATION: voiced (folds vibrate) vs. voiceless. ★ MANNERS: stop (oral/nasal via velum), fricative (frication), approximant (central/lateral), affricate (fricated-release plosive). CLASSES: obstruents (stops/fricatives/affricates), sonorants (nasals/approximants/taps/trills), continuants (fricatives/approximants). ★ VOWELS: height (vertical), backness (horizontal — central ≠ mid!), rounding (lips); + tenseness (tongue root: tense=advanced beat / lax=retracted bit), nasality (velum), length. Mono/di/triphthong. ★ IPA = one symbol per phone, [ ] phonetic vs. < > orthographic; principles > memorization. ★ SIGN PARAMETERS: HANDSHAPE, ORIENTATION, LOCATION, MOVEMENT (path = elbow/shoulder; local = wrist/knuckles). Minimal pair = differ in ONE parameter. Stokoe notation = first system. Nonmanuals matter. ★ SYLLABLE (σ): (onset) + NUCLEUS + (coda); open/closed/onsetless; SSP = sonority rises to nucleus, falls after. ★ STRESS: primary [ˈ] / secondary [ˌ] / unstressed; lexical (memorized) vs. predictable. ★ TONE (syllable/word meaning; H/L/M) vs. INTONATION (phrase/sentence function); f0 = pitch.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.12 Tone and intonation
notes.body: Vocal-fold vibration rate = fundamental frequency (f0), perceived as pitch. Tone = pitch used on syllables/words to change meaning; such a language is a tone/tonal language (e.g., Bemba lúk 'vomit' H vs. lùk 'weave' L). Many tone languages have H/L, some add a mid (M) tone; each syllable can carry its own tone. IPA notates tone with diacritics (´ high, ` low, ¯ mid), tone letters (˥ ˧ ˩), or non-IPA 1–5 numbers — all three appear in the literature, and each has ambiguity pitfalls. Intonation = pitch over phrases/sentences for conversational functions (statement vs. question); such a language is intonational.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.11 Stress
notes.body: Stress gives a syllable prominence via loudness, duration, and/or pitch (in sign: tension, quicker movement, longer holds). Levels: primary stress [ˈ], secondary stress [ˌ], and unstressed (e.g., ˈbʌ.niˌhʌɡ 'bunny hug'). Lexical stress is unpredictable and memorized (can make minimal pairs); predictable stress follows syllable-structure rules. Broad patterns: primary stress is nearly always within the first two or last two syllables — initial, peninitial, penultimate, ultimate (or antepenultimate). Secondary stress often alternates rhythmically. The 'stress-timed vs. syllable-timed' idea is not phonetically supported and best avoided.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.10 Syllables
notes.body: Syllables (σ) sit between words and phones. Structure: optional onset + required nucleus (usually a vowel, or a syllabic consonant like the end of bottle) + optional coda; onset/coda margins are simple (1 phone) or complex (2+). Open = no coda; closed = has coda; onsetless = no onset. CV-notation: e.g., approach = V.CCVC. Cross-linguistically, languages prefer onsets and disprefer codas, and prefer simple margins. Syllabification follows sonority; a sonority hierarchy ranks phones (vowels highest, obstruents lowest), and the Sonority Sequencing Principle (SSP) says sonority rises to the nucleus then falls ([plænt] obeys; *[lpætn] violates). Syllables may have psychological reality without consistent physical reality (hire vs. higher). Signs may also have syllable-like static (holds) vs. dynamic (movement) units — an open research question.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.9 Signed language notation
notes.body: There's no IPA-equivalent standard for signs. Stokoe notation (Stokoe 1960) was the first major system and proved signed languages have full linguistic structure; it analyzes signs by parameters (location, handshape, orientation, movement). Later, more iconic and language-neutral systems appeared: SignWriting and HamNoSys. None has become a universal standard, partly because they need special symbols with poor font support — which makes studying sign phonetics/phonology harder.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.8 Describing signs
notes.body: Signs are described by four parameters (primes): handshape (base-knuckle/interphalangeal configuration; unmarked = common/basic vs. marked), orientation (palm + finger direction, from the other four joints), location (where on the body/space; default = neutral signing space), and movement (path = elbow/shoulder through space; local = wrist/radioulnar/knuckles). One-handed signs use the dominant hand; two-handed signs add the nondominant hand (often the location). A minimal pair = two signs differing in exactly one parameter (SORRY/PLEASE differ in handshape; PROOF/STOP in orientation; APPLE/ONION in location; THINK/WONDER in movement). Chapter 4 extends minimal pairs to spoken languages.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.7 Signed language articulators
notes.body: The basic meaningful unit of a signed language is the sign (like a word). Unlike spoken words, signs don't clearly break into independent phone-like pieces — the hand's shape and location are inseparable. Two articulator groups: manual (arms, hands, fingers) and nonmanual (torso, head, face). Manual joints (shoulder, elbow, radioulnar, wrist, base knuckles, interphalangeal) move via abduction/adduction, flexion/extension, and rotation. Describe only the core movement of a sign, ignoring transitional movement into/out of it. Nonmanual articulation (brow, eyes, cheeks, head) is essential — a limitation of 'sign-language gloves,' which capture only some manual movement and burden deaf users.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.6 The IPA
notes.body: Segmentation = dividing a word into phones (easy for nab, hard for wool). Transcription notates phones unambiguously in square brackets [ ]; it can be broad or narrow. Writing-system symbols go in angle brackets < >. Ordinary spelling is unreliable (English <a> spells many vowels; the beat vowel is spelled i/ee/ea/e/y). The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA, est. 1886) gives one symbol per phone. Like the periodic table, its organizing principles matter more than memorizing symbols — knowing that [m] is a voiced bilabial nasal stop means knowing what those terms mean.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.5 Vowels
notes.body: Vowels are described by quality (a continuum): height (high beat / mid bet / low bat), backness (front beat / central but / back boot — don't confuse central with mid!), and rounding (rounded boot / unrounded — spread beat or neutral but). Extra properties: tenseness (tense = advanced tongue root, beat; lax = retracted, bit), nasality (oral vs. nasal/nasalized, e.g., bent), and length (long vs. short; long/short consonants = geminates/singletons). Dynamic vowels: monophthong (stable), diphthong (two qualities, e.g., toy), triphthong (three). Common description order: height–backness–rounding (with tenseness/length before, nasality after).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.4 Consonants: manner
notes.body: Manner = how air flows given the constriction. Stop = complete closure (oral stop with raised velum, e.g., plosives — plus ejectives/implosives/clicks; nasal stop with lowered velum). Fricative = narrow gap → turbulent frication (set, vet). Approximant = wide gap, little/no frication (central: yet/wet; lateral: let). Affricate = plosive with a slow, fricated release (jet). Also taps/flaps (very brief closure, e.g., North American 'atom') and trills. Classes: obstruents (oral stops + fricatives + affricates), sonorants (nasals, approximants, taps, trills), continuants (fricatives + approximants). Full description order: phonation–place–manner (e.g., met begins with a voiced bilabial nasal stop; set with a voiceless alveolar fricative).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.3 Consonants: place & phonation
notes.body: Consonants are constrictions: an active (lower) articulator moves toward a passive (upper) one. Active articulators (front→back): lower lip (labial), tongue tip (apical), blade (laminal), front (coronal), back (dorsal), root (radical), epiglottis (epiglottal). Passive articulators: upper lip, teeth (dental), alveolar ridge (alveolar), postalveolar, palate (palatal), velum (velar), uvula (uvular), pharyngeal wall (pharyngeal). Place of articulation = the active+passive combo, named active-first (e.g., labiodental = lower lip + upper teeth; often shortened, e.g., dorsovelar → velar). Special cases: bilabial, interdental, retroflex. The glottal place uses the vocal folds. In the larynx, the vocal folds can vibrate = voicing (voiced vs. voiceless); the broader category of vocal-fold airflow control is phonation.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.2 Speech articulators
notes.body: Articulation for speech happens in the vocal tract, shown in a midsagittal diagram (split down the middle; nostrils/lips on the left). Open regions: oral cavity, pharynx, nasal cavity. Below the pharynx: the trachea (windpipe → lungs; important) and esophagus (→ stomach; not used for speech). Individual speech sounds are phones (segments) — e.g., spill/slip/lisp/lips share four phones reordered. Whether a sound is a phone depends on whether it appears in ordinary words of that language (clicks are phones in isiZulu/Hadza but not English). The most fundamental split: consonants vs. vowels.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: 3.1 Modality
notes.body: Communication runs: message → articulation → linguistic signal → perception → reconstructed message. Modality = the whole physical chain of how a language is produced and perceived. Spoken languages are vocal-auditory (vocal tract → sound waves → hearing); signed languages are manual-visual (hands/arms → light waves → sight). Other modalities exist (e.g., manual-somatic tactile signing). Language is often multimodal (co-speech gesture; facial expression in sign). Phonetics is the study of modality in general (not just sound). Subfields: articulatory (how the body makes the signal — this chapter's focus), perceptual (how it's received), and acoustic (the sound waves themselves).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: Chapter 3 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 3 you should be able to: (1) identify the locations and functions of human anatomy relevant to articulating spoken and signed languages; (2) give articulatory descriptions of phones and signs; and (3) identify the meanings of many common IPA symbols.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 2
notes.body: ★ PERFORMATIVE speech acts DO things (Austin); Butler extends performativity to IDENTITY. Power needs authority + sincerity + uptake. ★ TABOO words are context-avoided; violating them causes OFFENSE. Taboos can be positive (respect) or negative. ★ OFFENSE = harm to hearers (impact); DEROGATION = utterer's disparaging attitude — INDEPENDENT of each other. ★ VULGARITY (bodily: shit) vs. EXPLETIVE (outburst: damn). ★ PARTICULARISTIC INSULT = one person for behavior; SLUR = a whole marginalized GROUP + POWER IMBALANCE → TOXICITY; slurs can be RECLAIMED (queer). ★ USE (refer) vs. MENTION (word as object, italics). ★ MATCHED-GUISE: hold STIMULUS constant, vary GUISE → rating difference = attitude toward the guise. ★ INDEXICAL BLEACHING = making a name 'sound more white'; DEADNAMING enforces power. ★ SPECIFIC singular 'they' = new change (unspecified singular they is ~600 yrs old); no one can stop language change. ★ VOCAL FRY/creak = normal phonation, policed in women. ★ STIGMA attaches to non-standard accents (accent itself is neutral); L2 accent shaped by L1; fix via PERCEPTUAL ADAPTATION. ★ LANGUAGE POLICY can erase or reinforce identity; residential-school prohibition = LINGUICIDE; Official Languages Act 1969 (FR/EN) ignored Indigenous languages; Indigenous Languages Act 2019.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.8 Exercise your linguistics skills
notes.body: Practice: (1) use morphology to compare 'standardized' vs. 'standard language' (what does -ize add, and why choose one term?); (2) reflect on feelings about your L2 accent and whether they trace to prestige/power; (3) examine which names/nicknames you use with different groups and why; (4) analyze swearing across contexts in terms of face (is positive or negative face threatened or enhanced?).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.7 Legally enshrined harms
notes.body: Governments use language policy to create unity or division. Canada's Official Languages Act (1969) recognized French and English and helped Francophones, but ignored Indigenous languages. Residential-school policies mandating English/French were a form of linguicide whose harms are ongoing. The 2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission led to the Indigenous Languages Act (2019) supporting reclamation. Tensions remain: Mary Simon (bilingual in English and Inuktitut) was criticized for limited French; Quebec's French-protection laws can suppress Indigenous and other languages (many Cree/Mohawk speakers use English, not French, as their L2).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.6 Linguistic law enforcement
notes.body: Unlike most social differences, deviating from a privileged language standard is openly policed. People police voices — criticizing 'uptalk' and vocal fry (creak), a normal low-frequency phonation disproportionately condemned in women even though men creak equally. People also police accents: a non-standard accent is stigmatized (the accent itself is neutral). L2 accents arise because the L2 grammar is shaped by L1 phonology. Stigma has real consequences (jobs, housing, courts, special-ed streaming, voice assistants). A UBC matched-guise study: the SAME voice was rated as more accented when paired with a Chinese-Canadian face — a mismatch of expectations. Remedy: perceptual adaptation — the more you attend to a talker/accent, the better you understand them.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.5 Pronouns, language change, and the grammar police
notes.body: Pronouns index identity. English third-person singular pronouns (it/he/she) give broad clues (thing/male/female) that can exclude people; 'they' avoids this. Unspecified singular 'they' is ~600 years old; the current change adds SPECIFIC singular 'they' for a known person. Because this tracks changing gender norms, prescriptivists resist it, but it keeps spreading (2015 ADS Word of the Year). A parallel: English lost thou/thee, leaving 'you' for both singular and plural. No one can stop language change, but users can speed it — using specific-singular-'they' reduces harmful misgendering.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.4 The power of names
notes.body: Names index social categories (gender, age, ethnicity). Matched-guise studies reveal hidden attitudes by holding a stimulus constant and varying its guise: identical résumés got fewer callbacks under non-English names (Oreopoulos 2011); Toronto landlords replied less to typically Arabic names. Names express identity and resistance — Indigenous name reclamation (e.g., Ta7talíya Nahanee, whose Sḵwx̱wú7mesh name uses '7' for the glottal stop) and trans naming. Deadnaming, forcible renaming, and mispronunciation enforce power (e.g., Black train porters all called 'George'; NDP leader Jagmeet Singh called 'Juggy'). Bucholtz calls making a name 'sound more English/white' indexical bleaching.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.3 Derogation, toxicity, and power imbalances
notes.body: Language expresses solidarity (e.g., Japanese honorific/endearment suffixes -san, -chan) but also harms. Offense = harm to discourse participants (impact); derogation/pejoration = the utterer's disparaging attitude. These are independent: 'shit' can offend without being derogatory; a coded slur ('Monday') can be derogatory without offending an unaware target. Particularistic insults (general pejoratives: jerk, idiot, asshole) target one person for specific behavior; slurs denigrate a whole marginalized GROUP and depend on a power imbalance, invoking historical violence — this is their toxicity. Insults aimed at high-status groups lack that force. Slurs can be reclaimed for solidarity (e.g., 'queer'; 'suffragette'). [Content note: discusses slurs.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.2 Language and offence
notes.body: Words carry emotional effects. Taboo words are avoided except in certain contexts; violating a taboo causes offence (e.g., 'shit' vs. innocuous 'poop'). Taboos arise for negative reasons OR positive ones (respect — e.g., Kambaata women avoiding sounds in in-laws' names). Taboo avoidance replaces a taboo word, either to avoid resembling it or to evoke it with a similar form ('sugar,' 'shoot'). The use–mention distinction matters: using 'shit' violates the taboo, but mentioning it as a linguistic object (in italics) usually doesn't — though for highly volatile words like racial slurs, even mentions can harm, so people use circumlocution or masking (s***, s-word). [Content note: swearing; brief mention of slurs.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: 2.1 Language and identity (performativity)
notes.body: Language can change the world. Performative speech acts (Austin) both convey information and perform an action ('I concede,' 'I now pronounce you married,' 'you're hired'). Their power depends on the authority and sincerity of the utterer plus the audience's uptake and society's agreement — a kid at recess saying 'I now pronounce you married' changes nothing. Butler extended performativity beyond speech acts: identity (e.g., gender) is a 'performative accomplishment' built through repeated social practice, including language. Saying 'eh' both expresses and reinforces a Canadian identity. Performativity ≠ acting/pretending — it means language performs functions that construct who we are.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: Chapter 2 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 2 you should be able to: (1) describe relationships between power and language across a variety of scenarios; (2) find real-world examples of language–power relationships; and (3) use metalinguistic awareness to interpret your own and others' attitudes about language.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 1
notes.body: ★ Linguistics = scientific, DESCRIPTIVE, EMPIRICAL study of human language. ★ 'Grammar' = the MENTAL system, not a rulebook; every language has one; none is 'better.' ★ Components: phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics (+ mental lexicon). ★ Form–meaning pairing is ARBITRARY (mostly). ★ Productivity/generativity = infinite output from finite means. ★ * marks an UNGRAMMATICAL form; grammaticality = what's POSSIBLE, not what exists. ★ Acceptability/grammaticality judgments are empirical DATA; other tools = surveys, corpora, experiments (Praat/ELAN, EEG, fMRI). ★ Standard = STANDARDIZED variety backed by social power, not linguistic superiority; bias/prestige intersect with race (Black English/AAVE). ★ Language science can do harm (missionary mis-documentation, residential schools, oralism) — practice HUMILITY. ★ LLMs are COMBINATORIAL (predict likely tokens via n-gram intuition/neural nets + RLHF); NO mind or communicative intent — unlike human generative, shared language. ★ Modality = spoken vs. signed; reading/writing are SECONDARY. ★ Implicit knowledge = unconscious grammatical knowledge; metalinguistic awareness = conscious knowledge about it.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.9 Exercise your linguistics skills
notes.body: Practice: (1) identify your L1(s) and make two descriptive (not prescriptive) observations; (2) evaluate invented product names — which are possible English words and why (phonotactic intuition); (3) coin new verbs from nouns/proper names ('Megabussing to Montreal,' 'got Pfizered') to illustrate generativity; (4) find a very new word and write a corpus-based dictionary definition.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.8 How do ChatBots synthesize sentences?
notes.body: LLMs trace back to Shannon (1948) and Markov (1913): the idea of an n-gram — the probability of the next item given previous ones (bigram QU is high-probability; a trigram like 'proud of ___' often predicts 'you'). Items are called tokens (letters, words, morphemes, punctuation). Real LLMs don't use raw n-grams but neural networks of weighted 'perceptrons' that predict likely next tokens. To avoid repetitive output, models sample among high-probability tokens (so outputs vary). After training, models are tuned with guardrails and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) — done by often underpaid, traumatized human labelers. Pronoun defaults (e.g., male doctor / female receptionist) show how training and rating choices bake in bias. Chatbots use 'I'/'you' to feel human, but they are not conversing.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.7 Do ChatBots have language?
notes.body: Human grammar is generative: a mind forms an idea, the body sends a signal, another mind interprets it, and a shared mental grammar makes mutual understanding possible. 'Generative AI' text generation relies on Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on huge corpora (often copyrighted, non-consensually scraped). An LLM has no mind or mental representation; it outputs statistically plausible word strings. Humans then can't help interpreting the output (like pareidolia). Human language is generative and shared to communicate meaning; LLM output is merely combinatorial, with no communicative intent — its 'meaning' is what humans attribute to it.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.6 Doing good with language science
notes.body: Linguistics skills apply widely: speech technology and reducing bias in speech recognition; language-learning apps; supporting Indigenous language reclamation (following community leadership, not as an outside 'saviour'); language teaching/ESL certification; and speech-language pathology (therapy after brain injury, gender-affirming voice work, accent coaching). Linguists also work in forensic linguistics, marketing/branding, authorship identification, and constructed languages for film/TV.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.5 Doing harm with language science
notes.body: Science is not inherently virtuous. Early 'linguistics' by missionaries mis-documented Indigenous languages through a Latin/European lens and 'froze' forms via writing; colonial governments then imposed English/French, including through residential schools where children were forbidden their languages and abused. Modern linguistics can also harm: extracting data without benefit to communities, publishing sensitive material, becoming an outside 'authority,' turning descriptions into prescriptions, and — via oralism — neglecting sign languages and mislabeling difference as 'disorder' (e.g., autistic 'pragmatic deficits' that vanished when autistic people talked with each other). Lesson: approach language science with humility. [Content note: residential schools, abuse.]
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.4 Standards and 'proper' grammar
notes.body: Everyone has linguistic biases. A 'standard' variety is really the standardized one that matches dictionaries/schools/high-status media, and its status comes from social power (e.g., the Académie Française; 'the Queen's English'), not linguistic superiority. Prestige and bias intersect with race: Standard American English implicitly means 'the way white people speak,' excluding varieties like Black English (AAL/AAVE). Treating the standardized form as the only 'correct' one discriminates against users of other varieties (examples: Kreyòl-speaking kids taught only in French; a judge distrusting a Nigerian-accented doctor).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.3 Studying language scientifically
notes.body: Doing linguistics scientifically means making systematic, empirical observations and taking a descriptive (not prescriptive) approach. A key tool is metalinguistic awareness — accessing conscious knowledge about your grammar. Acceptability/grammaticality judgments are empirical data: e.g., 'What did Sam compare the forged painting with?' is grammatical, but *'…and?' is not (marked with *). Other tools: surveys (regional variation, e.g., hoodie/bunny hug), corpora (large databases of real usage), specialized software (Praat, ELAN), and experiments (reaction times, eye-tracking, EEG, fMRI).
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.2 What grammars are and aren't
notes.body: 'Grammar' here means the mental system, not a rulebook. Every language has a grammar; claiming a language 'has no grammar' is a racist/colonialist/ableist move. No grammar, dialect, or variety is linguistically better than another — scientists describe, they don't rank. A core property is creativity/productivity/generativity: finite words + finite principles yield infinitely many sentences. Because grammar is productive, languages always change; complaints that young people 'ruin' a language are perennial and unfounded.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: 1.1 What even is language?
notes.body: Linguistics is the scientific study of human language. The word 'language' has several senses; linguistics focuses on human languages (spoken or signed), not computer or metaphorical 'languages.' Successful communication implies a shared system — the mental grammar. Its parts: the mental lexicon links forms to meanings (mostly an arbitrary pairing); articulatory phonetics governs producing sounds/signs; phonology governs how units combine and change; morphology handles meaningful pieces inside words; syntax combines words into phrases/sentences; semantics computes meaning; pragmatics handles meaning in context. Much grammatical knowledge is implicit (unconscious). Reading and writing are secondary — many languages and users have full grammars without literacy.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

notes.title: Chapter 1 — Learning Objectives
notes.body: By the end of Chapter 1 you should be able to: (1) differentiate prescriptive vs. descriptive ways of thinking about language; (2) identify the components of mental grammar; (3) explain properties shared by all human languages; (4) describe techniques for doing language science; and (5) discuss the ethics of doing language science.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]
